problem: Centralized multi-robot planners with a single LLM get overloaded as robots and environment complexity grow, while decentralized planners incur high communication and time costs. Single-view VLM multimodal CoT is unreliable because meaningless scene views disrupt reasoning.
motivation: House-service multi-robot systems need efficient cooperative exploration with low communication overhead and locally deployable models. The authors observe that if VLM CoT understands both the scene view and the robot's position on the global semantic map, decisions become more reliable, and the shared map can act as the communication channel.
key_idea: Use a decentralized per-robot VLM planner with cross-image multimodal CoT (scene view -> global semantic map with history nodes/frontiers), turning VLM Yes/No token probabilities into exploration/judgment scores, with the shared global semantic map as the only communication medium.
insight: Probability-based scoring of VLM outputs (Yes-token softmax) yields stable outputs and lets history-node scores be accumulated, balancing exploring frontiers versus returning to history nodes. Ablation (Table 3) shows each module helps: adding Perception CoT raises SR 0.677->0.698 (with Jud+Dec), and Logical Analysis is crucial (removing it gives SPL 0.286 vs 0.387 full). Detection/segmentation quality is the main bottleneck (GT-Seg raises SR from 0.716 to 0.872), and failure analysis shows detection failures dominate.
method: Visual Foundation Models: YOLOv10m detects objects with confidences, RedNet segments semantics; per-robot semantic maps are projected top-down and max-merged into a shared global semantic map used as the communication bridge.

Perception module: the VLM describes spatial relationships in the scene view, then a text-only CoT combining that description with detections asks whether the view is worth exploring; the normalized 'Yes' probability is the exploration score ES.

Judgment module: the VLM sees the global map annotated with the robot pose (red arrow), last goal, lettered history nodes and frontiers, plus the Perception CoT text; the 'Yes' probability (explore frontier) gives the judgment score JS.

HFOVS and history score: HFOVS = exp(τES·ES + τJS·JS) with τES=2, τJS=1; it is written into a 360-d angle vector per node/position, and the history score is the sum divided by the number of explorations within 25 pixels. HFOVS>=0.5 chooses frontier exploration, otherwise return to the history node with the highest HS.
Decision module: a second-stage CoT with a frontier-only annotated map plus Judgment output; the VLM outputs A/B/C/D and the token probabilities pick the frontier as the long-term goal.

Logical Analysis and Local Policy: if the previous goal is not reached and HFOVS<0.5, continue toward it; if the robot moved <25 pixels since last planning (collision trap), resample a random goal; an FMM planner outputs low-level actions.

setting.backbone: GLM-4V-9B (INT4-quantized, local, frozen) + YOLOv10m detector + RedNet segmenter
setting.training_data: none (training-free / zero-shot for planning; off-the-shelf pretrained detector and segmenter)
setting.action_space: 6 discrete actions: move forward 25cm, turn left/right 30°, look up/down 30°, stop; long-term goals on the map executed via FMM
setting.privileged: none for the main results; GT semantic segmentation (GT-Seg) variant uses ground-truth segmentation

numbers.extra: 2 robots, 500 steps, success dist 0.2m; HM3D v0.2 val 1000 episodes; multi-robot setting
numbers.evidence: Table 1: MCoCoNav (Ours) 0.387 SPL, 0.716 SR on HM3D v0.2
Table 6 / Table 2: MCoCoNav 0.297 SPL, 0.634 SR single-robot

numbers_note: Values printed as fractions in the paper were converted to percentages; evidence quotes keep the original form. Split is labeled 'val' as the paper says 'validation split'. HM3D v0.2 multi-robot setting.
results: With 2 robots, MCoCoNav reaches 0.387 SPL / 0.716 SR on HM3D v0.2 and 0.334 / 0.568 on MP3D, beating Co-NavGPT (0.331/0.661, GPT-3.5 remote) and Random Sampling (0.281/0.435 on MP3D) using only a local 9B VLM. Single-robot it gets 0.297 SPL / 0.634 SR, beating OpenFMNav and L3MVN; more robots improve SR/SPL at growing time cost.
limitations: Performance is bottlenecked by semantic segmentation/3D scan quality (detection failures dominate; GT-Seg gives a large gain), and detection traps rise with more robots.
Long runtime (about 10 days for a 2-robot HM3D evaluation on one RTX 3090) and time cost grows with robot count; only evaluated in simulation.
Relies on a hand-designed prompt and heuristic thresholds (25-pixel, 0.5) and simulated observations only.
